""Fear? Terror? Danger? No, it's called Democracy. Another Europe is possible".
General-turned-politician Roberto Vannacci, the leader of the new far-right National Future (FnV) party, was jubilant too.
"Europe is changing," Vannacci said. "Nessun dorma (let no one sleep)".
Italian opposition parties expressed alarm, saying the AfD's win showed the European Union is in peril.
"The 44% of the vote obtained by Alternative für Deutschland in Saxony is just not a local event," said Sandro Ruotolo, an MEP for the centre-left Democratic Party (PD)...

article.title: Saxony-Anhalt poll: 'A huge blow for the CDU, but also a huge win for the AfD'
article.summary: Carys Garland is pleased to welcome Markus Ziener, Visiting Senior Fellow at the German Marshall Fund. He interprets the AfD’s breakthrough in Saxony-Anhalt as a potentially historic turning point in post-war German politics. For Ziener, the significance lies not only in the scale of the far right’s electoral success, but also in the constituency behind it: many AfD voters, he argues, were previously politically disengaged rather than simply defecting from established parties. This complicates conventional explanations of the result as a straightforward transfer of support from the CDU to the AfD and raises a deeper question about the political expectations of a newly mobilised electorate.

article.title: The AfD’s win in Germany is a dark day for Europe. Time is running out to stop the far right | Cas Mudde
article.summary: This party is among the most extreme in Europe. To protect our democracies, liberal parties must urgently change their tacticsThe far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) narrowly failed to secure an outright majority in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt. But nobody should take comfort from that. The party still won by a landslide. Decades of far-right election gains have made them seem normal to the point where only the biggest victories are deemed newsworthy. But 44% of the vote for a party that is officially classified as “extreme right” is not normal. It is a black day for European democracy, even if it occurs in a small east German state.While Saxony-Anhalt (and Germany itself) may have dodged the worst outcome because the AfD won’t automatically fulfil its ambition of forming the first far-right state government in Germany since the Nazi era, there is no reason to assume it will be so lucky at the next election. article.title: Czech Politicians Divided Over AfD Victory in Saxony-Anhalt
article.summary: The Alternative for Germany (AfD) has secured a major victory in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, prompting different reactions from Czech politicians. While some have congratulated the party and called for dialogue with its leaders, others have warned that the result reflects the growing strength of political extremism. The result has also renewed debate in the Czech Republic over migration, security and how mainstream parties should respond to the AfD. Martin Kupka, chairman of the Civic Democratic Party (ODS), described the result as a warning for Europe. He said democratic parties could not counter extremist movements simply by labeling them or ignoring issues that concern voters. “Democratic parties must offer clear solutions: a tough migration policy, security, less regulation and no populist waste of public money,” Kupka said.
